title: No Names on the Label
subtitle: North Philadelphia and Washington, D.C.
focus: Doo-wop corners and Philly soul, the strings and house orchestras on the road to disco, and the live pocket of go-go on Washington's Black Broadway

intro.t: The New Jersey Turnpike, at the speed of a church van. Trucks pass you and honk. They think you're a choir. They're being supportive.
Reading the stub, for the record. Front: admit one, Harlem theater. Back, in Nana's hand: an address in North Philadelphia. And under it, underlined twice: 'Fridays.'
No name. Just the address and the day.
That's your grandmother. She don't give directions. She gives destinations.
Philadelphia. I remember Philadelphia. They put strings on me there. Violins, a harp, a whole orchestra in tuxedos. I looked expensive.
Listen. My cousin in Philly? Barber. Cuts hair like he's reading scripture.
Every barber in North Philly knows every old man in North Philly. That ain't relevant. That's infrastructure.
The address turns out to be a soul hall with half its marquee bulbs out and every one of its chandeliers on.

outro.t: Sunday, nine o'clock, a rest stop off the interstate. The first Sunday call home.
A sound man in Philly. A label with a lot of napkins. And a lawyer. She says there's a window, Nana, and it's nearly shut.
Silence on the line. Nana Dess can hold a silence the way other people hold a note.
Detroit gets cold at night even in June. Take a jacket.
She hangs up first. She always hangs up first.
I got a cousin in Detroit.
West, then. The Choir takes the long way. The Choir only knows the long way.

gigs.title: The Man Who Cut the Wax
gigs.blurb: A soul hall where the real band once played behind a curtain. The sound man is still here on Fridays.

vibe.label: Philly soul and the road to disco

challenge.text: Cut it hot: earn 8 stars over the set.

before.t: The North Philly Soul Hall. A mirror ball the size of a prize pumpkin, carpet the color of cherry soda, and a balcony that has held its breath since the sixties.
Promoter saw the van. He wants to know if y'all do hymns.
Not all the way through.
That's what I told him. He said that's most choirs.
At the soundboard, in a cardigan, sits a man of eighty-eight with a jeweler's loupe on a cord around his neck. He has not looked up since you walked in.
Excuse me, sir? Odessa Fontaine sent us. Sort of. She pointed.
He lifts the loupe and studies the ticket stub through it. He takes long enough to hum a whole chorus in. Nobody hums.
Pennington. Otis. Your grandmother sends me a Christmas card every year. No return address.
Then how do you know it's her?
I know it's her by the stamp. She buys the ones with the angel.
Can we ask you about a record?
You can ask. I don't answer people I haven't heard. Go on up. I'll hear you on my board.
Mr. Pennington, sir. My cousin cuts your hair.
A long pause. He squints at Cross through the loupe, as if Cross were a groove with a skip in it.
He takes too much off the back.
Every needle on his board is already set. He set them before you came in.

afterWin.t: He folds his headphones like a letter, goes to a back room, and comes out with a record in a plain paper sleeve.
Lantern L-1167. Side B. Don't look at the label. Look past it.
The smooth ring between the last groove and the label. The dead wax. He hands Tuesday the loupe.
A matrix number. And beside it, scratched in by hand... D. L. S. P. D.
Deacon. Low. Sister. Professor. Dess.
They told me no names on the label. Nobody said a thing about the wax.
Tuesday lays tracing paper over the dead wax and rubs it with the side of a pencil, gloves on, tongue between her teeth. Five letters come up grey out of nothing.
Nineteen sixty-eight, the Lantern Revue played this hall. Five pretty people out front, mouths moving. The real band played behind a curtain. Right there. I ran the sound.
I never saw their faces. Only their shoes, under the curtain. One more thing.
Another pause. He takes it slowly, the way you lower a needle onto something you can't afford to scratch.
Low kept a little book. Detroit boy.

afterLose.t: Hot is not the same as loud. Again.
He resets one needle. Just one. Run it back.

gigs.title: The Early Show
gigs.blurb: Lantern's own Watch Night 60 promo night. Invitation only, seven o'clock sharp, applause on cue.

challenge.text: Give the invited guests nothing to forgive: 90% on every song.

before.t: U Street, Washington. Seven o'clock sharp. The old theater is dressed in banners: WATCH NIGHT 60, a gold lantern on every one.
Manager needed a local opener for the label's promo night. I know a guy who knows the manager's cousin. Don't ask me which cousin.
Cousin. The lantern is on the banners. The napkins. The ice. Somebody put the logo on the ice.
On stage, The Birthrights soundcheck. Every note lands where it was told to. The lights hit their marks before the players do.
Their frontman, Kingston Lark, touches the monitor in his ear, the way other people knock on wood.
You're the opener.
We're {band}. Good to meet you.
Twenty-two minutes. Please keep to time.
We'll be done in twenty.
Twenty-two. There is a click.
Lark. Kingston Lark. As in the Lark on the label. As in A. Lark.
Listen. Nobody in this building knows who we are.
Good. Keep it that way.
The invited guests file in with lanyards and little plates. A light over the stage says APPLAUSE. They are waiting for it.

afterWin.t: Polite applause, exactly on cue. It starts when the light says start. It stops when the light says stop.
Backstage, a man in a grey suit holding a folder he never seems to put down.
Bryce Whitlock, Lantern Legacy. Lovely set. Just our standard appearance release, for the promo footage. Wherever you like.
Reading it, for the record. 'The performer grants...' 'in perpetuity...' and, small print, '...and all prior recordings in the performer's possession.'
All prior recordings in our possession. Cousin. That's the box.
We'll pass.
Of course. Keep that copy. We have plenty.
Evidence. Probably.
Your sound engineer in Philadelphia. He's eighty-eight?
He doesn't wait for an answer. Nobody told him about Philadelphia. Somebody told him about Philadelphia.
Manager says stick around. Eleven o'clock is for the neighborhood.

afterLose.t: Polite rooms are the hardest. Nobody tells you what's wrong.
Run it back, Pocket. They'll clap either way. Make them mean it.

gigs.title: The Late Show
gigs.blurb: Same stage, four hours later. The congas come out, and go-go does not believe in endings.

challenge.text: Hold the pocket: one streak of 300 notes, the way go-go never stops.

before.t: The banners are down. The lanyards went home. The neighborhood came in through the same doors and brought its own cowbell.
Congas, timbales and a cowbell turn up from nowhere. Local players sit in. Nobody booked them. Nobody would dare ask them to leave.
Now this is a room. Go-go don't believe in endings, Pocket. You stop, they keep going without you, and they talk about you while they do it.
At the end of the bar, a woman in red frames with a legal pad and a travel mug. She has been writing since the early show. She has not ordered anything.
Attorney Ngozi Pryce. I saw your early show. I came back for the real one.
Are you with the label?
No. That question was free. The next one is four hundred dollars.
I'm kidding. It's six.
Fun fact -
Forty dollars.
...I'll save it.
Why did you come back?
At seven o'clock you played like somebody was watching. I want to hear what you sound like when nobody's paying attention. Then I'll pay attention.
Eleven o'clock. The pocket opens. Nobody in this room has any plans to close it.

afterWin.t: Past one in the morning. The congas haven't stopped. They have no intention of stopping. You talk over them in a booth by the door.
We have a reel with five nicknames. A dead-wax rubbing with five letters. And a label that wants all prior recordings in our possession.
For the record. The law gives the makers of an old song one late window to take it back. It is nearly shut.
What do we need?
Bring me five names and one piece of paper Gus Lark didn't write.
There's more. On the reel, before the roll call, there's a man talking under the hiss. We can't make it out, but -
Then keep the man under the hiss to yourselves. Evidence you leak is evidence they prepare for.
Her phone buzzes. She reads it. Then she reads it again, which I suspect she never does.
Lantern is selling its catalogue to Perpetua Audio. The sale closes at midnight on Watch Night.
But that's -
The same night the window shuts. Yes.
Watch Night. My birthday. Somebody has booked my birthday and my funeral for the same midnight.

afterLose.t: Go-go forgives everything except stopping. Again. No charge.
The congas never stopped. Get back in.

afterChallenge.t: Watch Night, 1967. Twenty minutes to midnight. The pastor came down out of the pulpit and stood in the middle aisle.
He called out, 'Watchman, what of the night?' and the whole church called back that the morning was coming.
He asked again, and again, and every time the answer came back louder.
At 11:59 everybody knelt. The three out-of-towners in the back pew knelt too, and tried not to crease their revue trousers.
The bass player checked his watch on the way down and wrote something in a little book on his knee.
At midnight the church shouted. Not a cheer. A shout, the kind people save up for a whole year.
The guitar player hugged a stranger in the next pew, then the stranger's husband, then his mother, to be thorough.
And under all of it, up in the choir loft, the nineteen-year-old was humming her mother's tune. Not the printed one. Her mother's.
